frozen_original.title: Mar-a-Lago Settles Palm Beach Discrimination Lawsuit
frozen_original.synopsis: In 2013, Trump's Mar-a-Lago club settled a lawsuit alleging the club discriminated against Black and Jewish residents in Palm Beach County by restricting their membership and access to the club's facilities. The settlement required Mar-a-Lago to reaffirm its non-discrimination policies. This was part of a broader pattern: Trump had repeatedly positioned himself as a champion of diversity at Mar-a-Lago in contrast to other Palm Beach clubs, but his own properties faced recurring discrimination allegations throughout his career, from the 1973 housing case through multiple subsequent complaints.

primary.disposition: Corrected to the documented 1993 use agreement and its prospective-membership nondiscrimination clause. Research found no support for the supplied 2013 suit by residents; separate disputes include a 1996 Trump-filed claim against the Town.
primary.title: 1993 Mar-a-Lago Use Agreement Prohibited Membership Discrimination
primary.description_short: A 1993 Palm Beach agreement governing Mar-a-Lago's club use barred discrimination against prospective members on listed grounds.
primary.description_medium: On August 10, 1993, Donald Trump, Mar-a-Lago Club, Inc., and the Town of Palm Beach entered a Declaration of Use Agreement governing the property’s private-club use. The agreement prohibited discrimination against prospective members on enumerated grounds, including race and religion. The document supports a 1993 membership rule; it does not establish a 2013 discrimination lawsuit or settlement, or prove how the rule was enforced.
primary.description_long: On August 10, 1993, Donald J. Trump, the Town of Palm Beach, and The Mar-a-Lago Club, Inc. entered a Declaration of Use Agreement as the property was approved for use as a private social club. The recorded agreement says the Club “shall not discriminate against any prospective member” on listed grounds that include race, color, and religion. It set a nondiscrimination condition for prospective club membership. The document does not report a finding that Mar-a-Lago had discriminated, identify a plaintiff harmed by discrimination, or describe a 2013 lawsuit. PolitiFact’s review of a related but distinct Palm Beach dispute says Trump sued the town in 1996, alleging the town discriminated against Mar-a-Lago because it admitted Jewish and African American members; the town disputed that allegation. That was a claim by Trump against the town, not a case against the club brought by residents. This entry replaces the unsupported 2013-settlement story with the specific contractual clause established by the 1993 agreement. It does not infer whether the clause was enforced or whether it changed the club’s actual membership practices.

frozen_original.title: Trump Pardons Steve Bannon Before Trial on Fraud Charges
frozen_original.synopsis: On December 23, 2020, Trump pardoned Steve Bannon, his former chief White House strategist, who had been indicted in August 2020 on charges that he defrauded donors who gave over $25 million to the 'We Build the Wall' crowdfunding campaign, allegedly diverting funds to personal use. The pardon came before Bannon had even stood trial, eliminating the possibility of any federal conviction. Trump issued the pardon in the final hours before Christmas, minimizing media scrutiny. The pardon was widely criticized as protecting a key political ally from accountability and signaling that loyalty to Trump provided immunity from federal law enforcement.

frozen_original.title: DOGE Proposes Eliminating Social Security Disability Benefits
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, documents and public statements from Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency revealed proposals to eliminate or dramatically restructure Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) — the program that provides income support to over 8 million Americans with severe disabilities who cannot work. DOGE officials characterized SSDI recipients as lazy or fraudulent despite SSA data showing denial rates of over 60% and average annual benefits of approximately $16,000. The proposals included dramatically tightening medical eligibility criteria, shortening benefit periods, and converting SSDI from an earned benefit to a capped block grant. Disability rights organizations warned that implementing the proposals would force millions of severely ill and disabled Americans into destitution. The proposals provoked significant bipartisan congressional opposition.

primary.description_medium: The supplied record alleges that DOGE proposed eliminating or substantially restructuring Social Security Disability Insurance in March 2025. It lists tighter medical eligibility, shorter benefit periods, and a capped block grant, but supplies no proposal text or source. Search results documented separate SSA downsizing and service changes, which do not establish this SSDI proposal.
primary.description_long: The supplied record alleges that, in March 2025, officials associated with the Department of Government Efficiency proposed eliminating or sharply restructuring Social Security Disability Insurance. It further alleges proposals to tighten medical eligibility, shorten benefit periods, and replace the earned-benefit program with a capped block grant; the record also attributes disparaging comments about claimants to DOGE officials and describes warnings from disability-rights groups and bipartisan lawmakers. None of those specific proposal details is established by a source in the supplied packet. The search results found reporting about DOGE downsizing the Social Security Administration, closing offices, and changing service access, but those are distinct actions and do not prove a proposal to eliminate SSDI or convert it to a block grant. This draft keeps the policy claim in attributed, unverified form and does not present the reported recipient count, benefit amount, denial rate, rhetoric, or predicted effects as fact. The actual proposal, responsible official, date, text, and response remain unknown. This internal draft is not eligible for publication pending a direct document or credible report of the SSDI proposal.

survivor_record.title: Trump Claims Census Report Shows Noncitizens Voted in 2020 Election
survivor_record.synopsis: President Donald Trump has claimed that a census report shows 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. However, experts have questioned the analysis and validity of the report.
survivor_record.description_medium: On August 20, 2026, Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis claiming that about 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election and said it supported his claim that he won. Votebeat reported that election experts questioned the analysis because it omitted authors, detailed methods, and a margin of error. The outlet said the number, even if accurate, would not have changed the result. The Census Bureau did not respond to its request for comment.
survivor_record.description_long: On August 20, 2026, President Donald Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis that claimed, with high confidence, that approximately 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 presidential election. He said the result supported his repeated assertion that he had won that election. Votebeat reported that experts questioned the study's reliability because it did not identify its authors, explain the data's reliability in detail, or provide a margin of error. The analysis reportedly matched voter files with federal immigration records, and the data provider said it was surprised to see its files used for this purpose. The reported 24,000 figure represented less than 0.019% of the more than 128 million voters examined. Votebeat noted that even if the number were accurate, it was too small to change the outcome; it also said the analysis could not determine whether those voters supported Trump or Joe Biden. The Census Bureau did not respond to the outlet's request for comment. These distinctions matter: the report describes a government analysis and a presidential claim, alongside expert concerns about methodology. It does not establish that noncitizen voting affected the 2020 result.

accessed_source_evidence.source_excerpt: President Donald Trump this week unveiled another effort by his administration to raise questions about the outcome of the 2020 election he lost: an unusual U.S. Census Bureau analysis concluding with “high confidence” that 24,000 noncitizens illegally voted in the 2020 election. Trump touted the finding on social media and wrote that it supports his long-running false claims that he actually won the 2020 election. But experts said there are substantial questions about the Census Bureau study’s methodology and validity. And even if 24,000 noncitizens had voted in 2020, it wouldn’t have been enough to change the election’s outcome.
